title: Markets, Plans and Mixed Economies
objective: After this level you can compare market, planned and mixed economies.
summary: Markets spread decisions among buyers and sellers; command economies take goals from rulers. Hayek argued prices carry knowledge no planner can gather. Most real economies are mixed.

cards.headline: Tin gets scarce. Thousands of people use less of it. Nobody gave an order.
cards.body: Economist Friedrich Hayek posed that puzzle in 1945. Every economy has to decide what gets made. The real fight is over who decides: a planner, the market, or a bit of both.

items.label: Market economy
points: Decisions spread out among buyers and sellers

cards.headline: Prices as messages
cards.body: Hayek's argument: the knowledge an economy runs on exists in no single mind. It's scattered, with each person knowing things about their own resources that no planner ever can. Prices gather it up. When tin gets scarce, users don't need to know why. The price rises, and they use less. Hayek compared the price system to a kind of telecommunications system.

cards.fact: The inefficiency of communist economies helped bring down the Soviet Union in 1991.
cards.context: Soviet planners at Gosplan turned the party's goals into national plans. Hayek had argued no planner could gather knowledge scattered across a whole society. But markets don't run on prices alone either. Even market economies rely on government to protect property, enforce contracts, prevent fraud and collect taxes. That's why most real economies are mixed: part market, part government.

cards.headline: Who decides?
learned: Market economies spread decisions among buyers and sellers
Command economies take goals from rulers

questions.prompt: In a command economy, where do the economy's goals come from?

options.label: Village custom alone
options.rationale: A command economy runs on orders from above.

questions.explanation: In a command economy, economic effort serves goals handed down from a ruler or ruling class, like the Soviet Five-Year Plans.

questions.prompt: In Hayek's tin example, why do tin users cut back without knowing the cause?

options.label: A planner orders each factory to cut back
options.rationale: Hayek's point is that no order is needed.

options.label: They read about the shortage in the news
options.rationale: Most never learn why; they only see the price.

options.label: Tin becomes illegal to buy
options.rationale: Nothing is banned. The price does the work.

options.label: The rising price tells them to use less

questions.explanation: Prices carry scattered knowledge: users only need to see tin getting dearer to economize on it.

questions.prompt: Level 92's Marx inspired communist governments. What kind of economy did the Soviet Union run?

options.label: A command economy run through Five-Year Plans
A pure market economy with no planning
options.rationale: Soviet planners at Gosplan set national plans.

options.label: A barter economy with no money
options.rationale: The Soviet Union used money; its goals came from planners.

options.label: A gold standard economy
options.rationale: That's about money's backing, not who decides what gets made.

questions.explanation: Communist governments inspired by Marx ran command economies; the Soviet one began Five-Year Plans in 1928.
